the reduction of third-party appeal rights can be understood as a response to the juridification and complexity of planning law, and to the negative consequences for the government of a juridified and complex planning system.
in the Netherlands the access to the judicial review is being reduced, which is in line with the juridification thesis.
in a juridified planning system, government is reducing access to the legal process, and that it is doing this in order to limit the juridification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the regulatory state and the risk society.
the question whether the juridification and the reduction of appeal rights are compatible.
a fundamental paradox of the juridicalisation of planning: the more juridical the planning process becomes, the more the access to the law is restricted.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
juridification is a necessary condition for a regulatory state, but not a sufficient one.
the Dutch government is not only reducing third-party appeal rights, but that it is also reducing the quality of the land-use plan.
juridification is a fact of life in planning and that government is responding to this fact of life by taking away third-party appeal rights.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the juridification is a double-edged sword.
the Dutch planning system is becoming more and more legalistic while at the same time the legal system is becoming less and less available to citizens.
we are moving from a society of risk to a society of risk avoidance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulatory state and its consequences are not a one-way street.
we need to be aware that government is not only a source for law, but also for its reduction.
the juridification paradox can only be resolved by taking the juridification process as the object of policy-making.
